title: Angulimala, read whole
hook: the story from year one, now read in full

segments.voice: Yesterday: vanna, and Mahākaccāna's four tests: money, conduct, the law, going forth. Your line: not by birth.

Pasenadi of Kosala rides out of his capital with five hundred horsemen. His people have been gathering outside the palace, crying out about a killer in the forest, and the king is going to hunt Angulimāla down. On the way, he stops to pay respects to the Buddha. In year one, around day seventy, I told this story in pieces: the road, the chase, I have stopped, the woman in labor, the stones. Now the eighty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, read whole, and quieter scenes like this one come into view.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED HORSEMEN.` → `A KING ON A HUNT.` → `TOLD IN PIECES, NOW READ WHOLE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks him: what's wrong, great king? Is a neighboring kingdom attacking you? No, says Pasenadi. It's a bandit, Angulimāla. I'm going to put him down. Then the Buddha asks an unexpected question. Suppose you saw Angulimāla with his head shaved, in robes, gone forth, gentle, eating one meal a day, keeping the precepts. What would you do? The king says: I'd bow to him, offer him robes and food and shelter, and protect him. But how could someone like that ever become someone like this? The Buddha stretches out his arm and points. There is Angulimāla. The king is terrified, his hair standing on end. Don't be afraid, the Buddha says. You have nothing to fear from him. The king walks over, asks his family name, and offers him robes. Angulimāla says he already has his three. The king turns back to the Buddha and says it plainly: the one we couldn't tame with punishment or weapons, you've tamed without either. And he rides home. The sutta goes on: the woman in labor, the stones on the alms round, and then Angulimāla alone, freed, speaking verses. One is also in the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's words: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." In another verse he says his name had been Harmless, and now, at last, he lives up to it. Read whole, the story isn't only about one man stopping. A king stops too.
screen: `IS A KINGDOM ATTACKING YOU?` · `WHAT IF HE WERE A MONK?` · `THERE IS ANGULIMĀLA.` · `TAMED WITHOUT PUNISHMENT OR WEAPONS.` · then, large: `I HAVE STOPPED.`

segments.voice: If you have the Dhammapada or the sutta nearby, open it and read a few lines aloud, slowly; if not, say Müller's moon verse once, at the pace of a walk: he who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds. Then sit quietly with the picture of the moon coming out from behind a cloud.
Angulimāla. The killer who stopped, read whole: the Buddha on the road, the king with his army, and a man who finally lived up to his name, Harmless.
Your line: I have stopped. Tamed without punishment or weapons. Day four hundred seventy-one, done.

howItsDone: Angulimāla's verse of truth for a safe birth, the Aṅgulimāla Paritta, is still chanted by monks in Theravada countries for expectant mothers, and his story is told as proof that anyone can change.

what it means: read whole, it's also about a king who came to kill and went home, and a man who grew into his old name, Harmless.
what a scholar hears: MN 86, the Aṅgulimāla Sutta; his verses also appear in the Theragāthā, and the Dhammapada shares the moon verse.

chat.says: Did King Pasenadi ever catch the bandit Angulimāla?
options: No. He found him already a monk, tamed by the Buddha without punishment or weapons.
Yes: his five hundred horsemen captured him in the forest and punished him.
Yes: the Buddha handed him over to the king to face the court.
chat.meaning: In MN 86 the king finds Angulimāla gone forth, and says the Buddha tamed, without rod or weapon, the one he couldn't.

notes: MN 86 paraphrased; check the Pasenadi scene (five hundred horsemen, the hypothetical question, the king's fear, the offer of robes declined because Angulimāla has three, 'tamed without rod or weapon').

The name 'Harmless' (Ahiṃsaka) is from Angulimāla's own verse in MN 86; confirm.
Year-one days 71 to 74 told the chase, 'I have stopped', the birth and the stoning; this day avoids repeating them in detail.
